newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Fok the Sandman new powerbroker in Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Fok the Sandman new powerbroker in Hong Kong.

text.p: Some call tycoon Henry Fok the Godfather, others the Sandman. By whatever name, he's widely known as a man who pulls strings in the new Hong Kong.
He comes in from the cold of British disapproval to the warm embrace of Chinese rule with publication of the first post-colonial honours list.

He and 11 other notables identified by Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa will receive the Grand Bauhinia Medal -- the equivalent of a colonial knighthood -- from Chinese Vice-Premier Qian Qichen next week.
The "godfather' tag is testament to his mysterious past and powerful influence as the new Hong Kong takes shape.
"Sandman" refers not to a sleepy nature, but a lucrative sand monopoly bestowed by a grateful China upon one of its most trusted friends.
Fok, 74, brokered the China-backed bailout of chief executive Tung's shipping company in the mid-1980s, a deal that provoked accusations of puppetry from Hong Kong's vocal democratic lobby.

If Tung is a puppet, Fok is one of the people pulling his strings, diplomats say. He owns the apartment building that Tung chose to keep as his official residence instead of moving into the splendours of Government House.
Fok built up his business empire by shipping sand from southern China into Hong Kong, fuelling a construction boom.
By the time the late Chinese patriarch Deng Xiaoping had launched China on the road to capitalism with the reforms of the the late 1970s, Fok was already a kingpin.
The sand monopoly was issued in return for Fok's willingness to run goods into China past a U.N. embargo during the Korean War, diplomats say.
He was seen as a communist sympathiser by the British.
Now, as China prepares to celebrate the end of 156 years of British colonial rule, Henry Fok is starting to flex his powerful political muscles.
"I feel more free," he told the Asian Wall Street Journal.
In March, the tycoon jumped into the political fray over the Hong Kong government's management of property supply.

"Property prices are not just generally high, but are unacceptably high, to the extent that they are unrealistic and have affected commercial business," Fok, normally the soul of discretion, told China's parliament in a rare outburst.
"Hong Kong is no longer a shopping paradise. A lot of businesses have encountered difficulties because of the costly rent," he complained.

Political analysts said Fok, also vice-chairman of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, an advisory body, is bound to play a leading role as the economies of the Pearl River delta merge into one huge metropolis.

As interest mounts in the disposal of the US$19 billion Land Fund -- the cache of government property revenues designed to prevent the British stealing Hong Kong's silver when they leave at midnight on June 30 --- Fok and friends are poised to gain.
Improved transport links such as roads and high-speed trains are often cited as obvious targets for Land Fund cash.

"Think of 1978 and the (mass transit railway development)," one political analyst said. "The last generation's prosperity was built on infrastructure and consequent property development -- the MTR and (Kowloon-Canton railroad) and all the stations and property development spinning out from that."

Better links to southern China could help to solve Hong Kong's critical property shortage while joining the economies of the new Hong Kong and southern China -- and providing rich opportunities to those with established influence in the southern China region.
"It will be done," the analyst said. "It is as inevitable as the sun coming up tomorrow. Anybody paying attention will see this coming. That is the direction we're going."
